title: This Atlantic hurricane season is looking like a dud, but there will be a price to pay
gist: A strengthening El Niño is suppressing 2026 Atlantic hurricane activity to roughly 40 percent of normal accumulated cyclone energy, but climate scientists warn this same El Niño could be the strongest on record (potentially peaking near 3.6C, about 0.8C above the prior 2015-16 record), meaning the warming impact will lag into 2027 and make next year almost certainly the hottest ever recorded.

insights.claim: This year's accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) — a measure of overall tropical storm intensity and duration — is less than 30 percent of where it normally stands by early August; historically the Atlantic basin has usually seen three or four named storms by now, with one becoming a hurricane, but this year only two named storms (Arthur and Bertha) have formed, both middle-of-the-road in intensity.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified below-normal ACE reading (under 30% of typical) gives insurers, coastal real estate markets, and energy/commodity traders a concrete data point for near-term hurricane-risk pricing this season.
insights.locator: Why this season should be below normal

insights.claim: Seasonal hurricane forecaster Phil Klotzbach at Colorado State University has steadily revised his outlook downward: in April he predicted 13 named storms and six hurricanes, but his latest and final outlook (issued Wednesday) predicts only nine named storms and four hurricanes, with accumulated cyclone energy expected to be only about 40 percent of normal.
insights.speaker: Phil Klotzbach (via Eric Berger)
insights.so_what: A ~30% downward revision in named-storm count from a leading named forecaster over four months is a specific, trackable forecast series relevant to reinsurance pricing and Gulf/Atlantic coast risk models for the remainder of the 2026 season.

insights.claim: Klotzbach said the primary reason for the quiet season is a rapidly strengthening El Niño in the equatorial Pacific, which drives higher wind shear across the Atlantic basin — the region where most hurricanes form and intensify — and that his team is forecasting a well-below-average probability of major hurricane landfalls along the continental US coastline and in the Caribbean.
insights.speaker: Phil Klotzbach (via Eric Berger)
insights.so_what: The causal mechanism (El Niño-driven Atlantic wind shear suppressing hurricanes) is the load-bearing claim for the below-average landfall probability forecast — useful context for anyone modeling Gulf Coast energy infrastructure or coastal property risk this season.
insights.quote: We are extremely confident that we will have a strong El Niño for the peak of hurricane season.

themes.theme: The record-breaking El Niño and its deferred cost

insights.claim: Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather, who writes at The Climate Brink newsletter, said the multi-model median for this El Niño event's peak currently stands at 3.6C, roughly 0.8C hotter than the prior record of 2.75C set in 2015-16, noting that the gap between the strongest and fifth-strongest El Niño of the past 150 years is only about 0.5C — meaning current models are forecasting something outside the envelope of anything ever observed.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather (via Eric Berger)
insights.so_what: A projected El Niño peak 0.8C above the prior all-time record, when the normal spread between the top five historical events is only 0.5C, is a statistically extreme outlier forecast — a strong quantitative signal for climate-risk modelers and commodity/insurance markets tracking global weather volatility.
insights.quote: The multi-model median for the event’s peak currently stands at 3.6C, roughly 0.8C hotter than the prior record of 2.75C set in 2015-16.

insights.claim: El Niño's global warming impact typically lags its peak by several months, meaning the bulk of associated global heating will be observed in 2027, and the article concludes that global temperatures next year will 'almost certainly' be the hottest ever recorded — and possibly not close.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: This is a specific, near-term calendar prediction (2027 as likely hottest year on record) with a defined causal lag mechanism, giving a concrete forward-looking marker for climate-risk, agriculture, energy-demand, and insurance-pricing models to track against.

insights.claim: A quiet Atlantic hurricane season and a record-strength El Niño are causally linked but represent a tradeoff: fewer storms threaten the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts this year, but the same El Niño driving that quiet season is expected to add substantial additional fuel to already-rising global temperatures.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: This is the article's central thesis and the reason for its headline framing ('a price to pay') — investors and risk managers should not read a quiet hurricane season as an unambiguous positive, since it is a symptom of the same climate driver that is expected to produce record global heat in the following year.
